modern: When sin is pardoned, our greatest sorrow is over, and our truest pleasure begins. The joy the Lord gives his reconciled ones is so great that it overflows and fills all nature with delight. The material world has hidden music in it, and a renewed heart knows how to bring it out and give it a voice. Creation is the organ, and a gracious person finds its keys, lays his hand on them, and wakes the whole system of the universe to the harmony of praise. Mountains and hills and other great things are, so to speak, the bass of the chorus, while the trees of the wood and everything that has life take up the melody of the song.

When God’s Word prospers among us, and souls are saved, everything seems full of song. When we hear the confessions of young believers and the testimonies of well-taught saints, we’re made so happy that we must praise the Lord, and then it seems as if rocks and hills, woods and fields echo our notes of joy and turn the world into an orchestra. Lord, on this happy May Day, lead me out into your musical world, as full of praise as a lark in full song.

notes.term: The mountains and the hills shall break forth
notes.note: The verse begins, “For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace” ([[Isa.55.12|Isaiah 55:12]]).
Hidden, present but not yet heard.
Given a voice; heard aloud.
The melody, the tune.

notes.term: God’s Word is made to prosper
notes.note: “It shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it” ([[Isa.55.11|Isaiah 55:11]]).
May 1, an old spring holiday in England.

modern: Sowing looks like a losing business, for we put good grain into the ground, never to see it again. Sowing to the Spirit seems a very fanciful, dreamy business, for we deny ourselves and seem to get nothing for it. Yet if we sow to the Spirit by working to live for God, seeking to obey God’s will, and spending ourselves to promote his honor, we won’t sow in vain. Life will be our reward, even everlasting life. We enjoy it here as we come to know God, have fellowship with God and enjoy God. This life flows on like an ever-deepening, ever-widening river, until it carries us to the ocean of infinite happiness, where the life of God is ours forever and ever.

Let’s not sow to our flesh today, for the harvest will be decay, since the flesh always tends that way. But with holy self-mastery, let’s live for the highest, purest and most spiritual ends, seeking to honor our most holy Lord by obeying his most gracious Spirit. What a harvest it will be when we reap everlasting life! What sheaves of endless bliss will be reaped! What a festival that harvest will be! Lord, make us such reapers, for your Son’s sake.

notes.term: He that soweth to the Spirit
notes.note: “Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption” ([[Gal.6.7-Gal.6.8|Galatians 6:7–8]]).
Grain of any kind, such as wheat or barley.
Making it our aim, taking pains.
Close fellowship and sharing, with God or with each other. (Also the Lord’s Supper.)
Happiness, bliss.
The flesh reaps decay and ruin ([[Gal.6.8|Galatians 6:8]]).

modern: There are signs of the Lord moving that should move us. The Spirit of God blows where he pleases, and we hear the sound of it. That’s the time for us to be more active than ever. We must seize the golden opportunity and make the most of it. It’s our job to fight the Philistines at all times; but when the Lord himself goes out ahead of us, then we should be especially brave in the war.

The breeze stirred the treetops, and David and his men took it as the signal to attack; and as they advanced, the Lord himself struck down the Philistines. Oh, that today the Lord would give us an opening to speak for him with many of our friends! Let’s be on the watch to make use of the hopeful opening when it comes. Who knows but that this may be a day of good news, a season of winning souls? Let’s keep our ears open to hear the rustle of the wind, and our minds ready to obey the signal. Isn’t this promise, “then shall the Lord go out before thee,” encouragement enough to play the man? Since the Lord goes ahead of us, we don’t dare hold back.

notes.term: The sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees
notes.note: The sound of marching in the treetops, God’s signal to David to attack the Philistines ([[2Sam.5.22-2Sam.5.25|2 Samuel 5:22–25]]).
Get moving.
An army.
Where he pleases. “The wind bloweth where it listeth” ([[John.3.8|John 3:8]]).
Up and active.
Brave.
Act bravely. “Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people” ([[2Sam.10.12|2 Samuel 10:12]]).

modern: This may express the feelings of a man or woman downtrodden and oppressed. Our enemy may put out our light for a while. There is sure hope for us in the Lord, and if we’re trusting in him and holding on to our integrity, our time of being cast down and in darkness will soon be over. The enemy’s insults last only a moment. The Lord will soon turn their laughter into lament, and our sighing into singing.

What if the great enemy of souls should triumph over us for a while, as he has triumphed over better people than we are? Still, let’s take heart, for we’ll overcome him before long. We’ll rise from our fall, for our God hasn’t fallen, and he’ll lift us up. We won’t stay in darkness, although for now we sit in it, because our Lord is the fountain of light, and he’ll soon bring us a joyful day. Let’s not despair, or even doubt. One turn of the wheel, and the lowest will be at the top. Woe to those who laugh now, for they’ll mourn and weep when their boasting is turned into everlasting contempt. But blessed are all holy mourners, for they’ll be comforted by God.

notes.term: Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy

notes.note: Being cast down, discouraged.
Mourning, crying out in grief.
Remain, stay.
The old picture of fortune’s wheel, which can bring the lowest to the top in a moment.

notes.term: Woe unto those who laugh now
notes.note: “Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep” ([[Luke.6.25|Luke 6:25]]).
“Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted” ([[Matt.5.4|Matthew 5:4]]).

modern: God’s own people may sell themselves into captivity by sin. This is a very bitter fruit from an exceedingly bitter root. What slavery it is when a child of God is sold under sin, held in chains by Satan, robbed of his freedom, of his power in prayer and of his delight in the Lord! Let’s watch that we don’t come into such slavery. But if this has already happened to us, let’s by no means despair.

We can’t be held in slavery forever. The Lord Jesus has paid too high a price for our redemption to leave us in the enemy’s hand. The way to freedom is, “Return unto the Lord thy God.” Where we first found salvation, we’ll find it again. At the foot of Christ’s cross, confessing sin, we’ll find pardon and deliverance. What’s more, the Lord wants us to obey his voice in everything he has commanded us, and we must do this with all our heart and all our soul; and then our captivity will end.

Often low spirits and great misery of soul are taken away as soon as we leave our idols and bow in obedience before the living God. We don’t need to stay captives. We may return to our citizenship in Zion, and do it quickly. Lord, turn our captivity!

notes.note: Bring you back from exile, restore your fortunes. Moses promised this to Israel if they returned to God in their scattering ([[Deut.30.1-Deut.30.3|Deuteronomy 30:1–3]]).
“And shalt return unto the LORD thy God, and shalt obey his voice according to all that I command thee… with all thine heart, and with all thy soul” ([[Deut.30.2|Deuteronomy 30:2]]).
Leave, give up.
Jerusalem, the city of God; here, the company of God’s people.
Quickly.

modern: When we see the wicked prosper, we’re inclined to envy them. When we hear the noise of their fun while our own spirit is heavy, we half think they have the best of it. This is foolish and sinful. If we knew them better, and especially if we remembered how they will end, we’d pity them.

The cure for envy lies in living with a constant sense of God’s presence, worshiping God and having fellowship with him all day long, however long the day may seem. True religion lifts the soul into a higher region, where judgment becomes clearer and desires are lifted higher. The more of heaven there is in our lives, the less of earth we’ll covet. The fear of God drives out envy of people.

The deathblow to envy is calmly thinking about the future. The wealth and glory of the ungodly are an empty show. This showy display flashes out for an hour and then goes out. What good does his prosperity do the prosperous sinner when judgment catches up with him? As for the godly person, his end is peace and blessedness, and no one can rob him of his joy. So let him give up envy and be filled with sweet contentment.

notes.term: Let not thine heart envy sinners

notes.note: Asaph envied the wicked “until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end” ([[Ps.73.3|Psalm 73:3]]; [[Ps.73.17|73:17]]).
Fun, merriment.
Talking closely together.
Want what belongs to someone else.
“Surely every man walketh in a vain shew” ([[Ps.39.6|Psalm 39:6]]).
“Mark the perfect man… for the end of that man is peace” ([[Ps.37.37|Psalm 37:37]]).
Give up, go without.

modern: Israel had to conquer idol-worshiping cities and destroy all the plunder, treating everything polluted by idolatry as a cursed thing to be burned with fire. Now Christians must treat every kind of sin the same way. We mustn’t let a single evil habit remain. It’s war to the knife now with sins of every kind and size, whether of the body, the mind or the spirit. We don’t think of this giving up of evil as deserving mercy, but we see it as a fruit of God’s grace, which we wouldn’t miss for anything.

When God makes us have no mercy on our sins, then he has great mercy on us. When we’re angry with evil, God is no longer angry with us. When we multiply our efforts against sin, the Lord multiplies our blessings. The way of peace, of growth, of safety, of joy in Christ Jesus will be found by following these words: “There shall nought of the cursed thing cleave to thine hand.” Lord, purify me today. Compassion, prosperity, increase and joy will surely be given to those who put away sin with solemn resolve.

notes.note: A city in Israel that turned to other gods was to be destroyed with all its spoil ([[Deut.13.12-Deut.13.17|Deuteronomy 13:12–17]]).
Cling, stick.
Nothing.
What God had devoted to destruction. Achan kept some of it from Jericho and brought disaster on Israel ([[Josh.7.1|Joshua 7:1]]).
Plunder taken in war.
A fight to the death, with no truce.
Sin, wickedness.

modern: Yes, there’s work in Christ’s vineyard for old folks. It’s the eleventh hour, and yet he’ll let us work. What great grace this is! Surely every old man ought to jump at this invitation! Once people are getting on in years, nobody wants them as workers; they go from shop to shop, and employers look at their gray hair and shake their heads. But Jesus will hire old people, and pay them good wages too! This is mercy indeed. Lord, help the elderly to enlist in your service without an hour’s delay.

But will the Lord pay wages to worn-out old men? Don’t doubt it. He says he’ll give you whatever is right if you’ll work in his field. He’ll surely give you grace here and glory hereafter. He’ll give present comfort and future rest; strength to match your day, and a vision of glory when the night of death comes on. The Lord Jesus will give all these as freely to someone converted in old age as to one who enters his service young.
Let me tell this to some unsaved old man or old woman, and pray the Lord to bless it, for Jesus’ sake. Where can I find such people? I’ll be on the lookout for them, and kindly tell them the news.

notes.note: In Jesus’ story, the owner of a vineyard hires workers even at the eleventh hour, an hour before the day’s work ends, and pays them a full day’s wage ([[Matt.20.6-Matt.20.9|Matthew 20:6–9]]).
Old people. “Body” once meant a person, as it still does in “somebody”.
Old.
Hire.
“The LORD will give grace and glory” ([[Ps.84.11|Psalm 84:11]]). Hereafter means in the life to come.
“As thy days, so shall thy strength be” ([[Deut.33.25|Deuteronomy 33:25]]).
Someone who has turned to Christ.

modern: The root of faith grows the flower of joy in the heart. We may not rejoice at first, but joy comes in due time. We trust the Lord when we’re sad, and in due season he answers our confidence so well that our faith turns into fulfillment and we rejoice in the Lord. Doubt breeds distress, but trust means joy in the long run.

The assurance the psalmist expresses in this verse is really a promise held out in the hands of holy confidence. Oh, for grace to take hold of it as our own! If we don’t rejoice right now, we will, as surely as David’s God is our God.

Let’s think deeply about the Lord’s holy name, so that we may trust him better and rejoice more readily. In character he is holy, just, true, gracious, faithful and unchanging. Isn’t a God like that to be trusted? He is all-wise, almighty and present everywhere; can’t we cheerfully rely on him? Yes, we will, at once, and without holding anything back. Jehovah-Jireh will provide, Jehovah-Shalom will send peace, Jehovah-Tsidkenu will justify, Jehovah-Shammah will be near forever, and in Jehovah-Nissi we’ll conquer every foe. Those who know your name will trust you; and those who trust you will rejoice in you, O Lord.

notes.note: Enjoying what was hoped for; fulfillment.
Take as your own.
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles. Spurgeon names five of the titles built on it.
“The LORD will provide”: Abraham’s name for the mountain where God provided a ram in Isaac’s place ([[Gen.22.14|Genesis 22:14]]).
“The LORD is peace”: Gideon’s name for his altar ([[Judg.6.24|Judges 6:24]]).
“The LORD our righteousness” ([[Jer.23.6|Jeremiah 23:6]]).
“The LORD is there”: the name of the city in Ezekiel’s vision ([[Ezek.48.35|Ezekiel 48:35]]).
“The LORD is my banner”: Moses’ name for his altar after the victory over Amalek ([[Exod.17.15|Exodus 17:15]]).
“They that know thy name will put their trust in thee” ([[Ps.9.10|Psalm 9:10]]).

modern: Because God will never leave us or forsake us, we may well be content with what we have. Since the Lord is ours, we can’t be left without a friend, a treasure and a home. This assurance can make us feel quite independent of people. With so high a protector we aren’t tempted to grovel before others and ask their permission to call our lives our own; whatever we say, we say boldly, and we dare anyone to contradict it.

Whoever fears God has nothing else to fear. We should stand in such awe of the living Lord that all the threats the proudest persecutor can make have no more effect on us than the whistling of the wind. People today can’t do as much against us as they could when the apostle wrote the verse at the top of this page. The rack and the stake have gone out of fashion. Giant Pope can’t burn the pilgrims now. If the followers of false teachers try cruel mockery and scorn, we aren’t surprised, for the people of this world can’t love the heavenly seed. So what? We must put up with the world’s scorn. It breaks no bones. With God’s help, let’s be bold; and when the world rages, let it rage, but let’s not fear it.

notes.note: “Be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” ([[Heb.13.5|Hebrews 13:5]]).
Support and protection from someone powerful.
Bow and scrape; grovel.
Instruments of torture and execution. The rack stretched a prisoner’s body; martyrs were burned at the stake.
In John Bunyan’s *The Pilgrim’s Progress*, Christian passes the cave of two giants, Pope and Pagan, who once killed pilgrims. Pope is now too old and stiff to do more than mutter at them.
God’s people, born from above.

modern: Some of us have been like the tribe of Gad. For a while our enemies were too many for us; they came at us like a raiding band. Yes, and for the moment they beat us, and gloated over their passing victory. In this they only proved that the first part of the family inheritance really is ours, for Christ’s people, like Gad, will have a troop overcoming them. Being overcome like this is very painful, and we’d have despaired if we hadn’t believed, by faith, the second line of our father’s blessing: “He shall overcome at the last.” “All’s well that ends well,” said the world’s poet, and he spoke the truth. A war is to be judged, not by its first wins or losses, but by what happens “at the last.” The Lord will give truth and righteousness the victory “at the last”; and as Mr. Bunyan says, that means forever, for nothing can come after the last.

What we need is patient perseverance in doing good, and calm confidence in our glorious Captain. Christ, our Lord Jesus, wants to teach us his holy skill of setting the face like a flint, to see a work or a suffering through until we can say, “It is finished.” Hallelujah. Victory! Victory! We believe the promise: “He shall overcome at the last.”

notes.note: Jacob’s blessing on his son Gad, whose name sounds like the Hebrew for “troop” ([[Gen.49.19|Genesis 49:19]]). A troop here is a raiding band.
A slip in the original: the troop is Gad’s blessing, not Dan’s.
A blessing.
The title of a play by Shakespeare, “the world’s poet”.
John Bunyan (1628–1688), the Puritan preacher who wrote *The Pilgrim’s Progress*.
Christ as the leader of his people: “the captain of their salvation” ([[Heb.2.10|Hebrews 2:10]]).

notes.term: Setting the face like a flint
notes.note: Firm determination. “Therefore have I set my face like a flint” ([[Isa.50.7|Isaiah 50:7]]); Jesus “stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem” ([[Luke.9.51|Luke 9:51]]).
Jesus’ cry from the cross ([[John.19.30|John 19:30]]).

modern: Whoever tends the fig tree gets figs for his trouble, and whoever waits on a good master is rewarded with honor. The Lord Jesus truly is the very best of masters, and it’s an honor to be allowed to do the smallest thing for his sake. To serve some lords is to look after a crab-apple tree and eat sour crab apples as your wages; but to serve my Lord Jesus is to keep a fig tree of the sweetest figs. His service is a delight in itself; staying in it is promotion; success in it is blessedness here below; and its reward is glory above.

Our greatest honors will be gathered in the season when the figs are ripe, that is, in the next world. Angels who serve us now will carry us home when our day’s work is done. Heaven, where Jesus is, will be our honored mansion, eternal bliss our honored portion, and the Lord himself our honored companion. Who can imagine the full meaning of this promise, “He that waiteth on his master shall be honored”?
Lord, help me to wait on my Master. Let me leave all thought of honor to the hour when you yourself will honor me. May your Holy Spirit make me a humble and patient worker and waiter!

notes.note: Serves; attends to.
A crab-apple tree, whose small fruit is sour.
Servants, attendants. Angels are “ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation” ([[Heb.1.14|Hebrews 1:14]]).
When the beggar Lazarus died, he “was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom” ([[Luke.16.22|Luke 16:22]]).
A dwelling place. “In my Father’s house are many mansions” ([[John.14.2|John 14:2]]).
A share of an inheritance. When God is “our portion”, he himself is what we inherit, and he is enough.

modern: Until the day breaks and the shadows flee away, what a blessing it is to see in Jesus “the morning star”! I remember when the newspapers carried the silly story that the star of Bethlehem had appeared again. When we looked into it, we found it was only “the morning star”; but no great mistake had been made after all.

It’s best to see Jesus as the sun; but when we can’t, the next best thing is to see him as the star that promises the day and shows that the eternal light is close at hand. If today I’m not all I hope to be, still I see Jesus, and that assures me that one day I’ll be like him. A sight of Jesus by faith is the guarantee that I’ll see him in his glory and be changed into his image. If I don’t have all the light and joy I could wish for right now, I will have it; for as surely as I see the morning star, I’ll see the day. The morning star is never far from the sun.

Come, my soul, has the Lord given you the morning star? Are you holding on to the truth, grace, hope and love that the Lord has given you? Then in this you have the dawn of coming glory. He who makes you overcome evil and keep on in righteousness has given you the morning star in doing so.

notes.note: The planet Venus, bright in the east just before sunrise. Christ promises it to “him that overcometh” ([[Rev.2.26-Rev.2.28|Revelation 2:26–28]]) and calls himself “the bright and morning star” ([[Rev.22.16|Revelation 22:16]]).
“Until the day break, and the shadows flee away” ([[Song.2.17|Song of Solomon 2:17]]).
A silly, baseless story.
The star that led the wise men to the infant Jesus ([[Matt.2.9|Matthew 2:9]]).
“We shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” ([[1John.3.2|1 John 3:2]]).
“We all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image” ([[2Cor.3.18|2 Corinthians 3:18]]).

modern: It’s the Lord’s way to tear before he heals. This is the honest love of his heart and the sure surgery of his hand. He also bruises before he binds up, or else the work would be uncertain. The law comes before the gospel; the sense of need before the supply of it. Are you, reader, under the convincing, crushing hand of the Spirit right now? Have you received the spirit of bondage again to fear? This is a healthy first step toward real gospel healing and binding up.

Don’t despair, dear heart, but come to the Lord with all your jagged wounds, black bruises and running sores. He alone can heal, and he loves to do it. It’s our Lord’s work to bind up the brokenhearted, and he is gloriously at home in it. Let’s not linger, but at once return to the Lord we have wandered from. Let’s show him our gaping wounds, and beg him to recognize his own work and finish it. Will a surgeon make a cut and then leave his patient to bleed to death? Will the Lord pull down our old house and then refuse to build us a better one? Do you ever needlessly add to the misery of poor anxious souls? Far be it from you, O Lord.

notes.note: Struck.
Here, convicting: showing us our sin and making us feel it.

notes.term: The spirit of bondage again to fear
notes.note: The fear of a slave who expects punishment. “Ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption” ([[Rom.8.15|Romans 8:15]]).
Good for you; healing.
A first step.
“He hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted” ([[Isa.61.1|Isaiah 61:1]]).
Beg.
Needlessly; without cause.
An old way of saying “you would never do such a thing”, as Abraham said to God ([[Gen.18.25|Genesis 18:25]]).

modern: Does the Lord say this to me? Yes, if I have known his name. Blessed be the Lord, I’m no stranger to him. I have tried him, and proved him, and known him, and so I trust him. I know his name as a sin-hating God, for by his Spirit’s convincing power I’ve been taught that he will never wink at evil. But I also know him as the sin-pardoning God in Christ Jesus, for he has forgiven me all my sins. His name is faithfulness, and I know it, for he has never forsaken me, though my troubles have multiplied.

This knowledge is a gift of grace, and the Lord makes it the reason he gives another gift of grace, namely, setting us on high. This is grace upon grace. Notice that if we climb up high, the position may be dangerous; but if the Lord sets us there, it’s safe. He may raise us to great usefulness, to rich experience, to success in service, to leadership among workers, to a father’s place among the little ones. If he doesn’t do this, he may set us on high by close fellowship, clear insight, holy triumph, and a gracious foretaste of eternal glory. When God sets us on high, Satan himself can’t pull us down. Oh, may this be our case all through this day!

notes.term: I will set him on high
notes.note: “Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name” ([[Ps.91.14|Psalm 91:14]]). Set high, out of danger’s reach.
Tested, and found true.
Here, convicting: showing us our sin and making us feel it.
Pretend not to see; overlook.
Sins; wrongs.
“Of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace” ([[John.1.16|John 1:16]]).
Outstanding; of a high order.

modern: It isn’t right that the man who won’t forgive should be forgiven, and whoever won’t give to the poor won’t have his own needs relieved. God will measure to us with our own measuring baskets; and those who have been hard masters and hard creditors will find that the Lord deals hard with them. “He shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy.”

Today let’s try to give and to forgive. Let’s remember the two bears: bear and forbear. Let’s be kind and gentle and tender. Let’s not put a harsh meaning on how people act, or drive hard bargains, or pick foolish quarrels, or be hard to please. Surely we want to be blessed, and we also want to obtain mercy: so let’s be merciful, that we may have mercy. Let’s meet the condition, so that we may win the blessing. Isn’t it a pleasant duty to be kind? Isn’t there far more sweetness in it than in being angry and ungenerous? Why, there’s a blessedness in the thing itself! And besides, obtaining mercy is a rich reward. What but sovereign grace could think of a promise like this? We’re merciful to our fellow mortals in pennies, and the Lord forgives us “all that debt.”

notes.note: Suitable, fitting.
A bushel was a basket used to measure grain. “With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again” ([[Matt.7.2|Matthew 7:2]]).
“For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy” ([[Jas.2.13|James 2:13]]). “Shewed” is an old spelling of showed.
An old saying: put up with wrongs, and hold back from paying them back.
Interpretations; the meaning we put on something.
A blessing; one of the “Blessed are…” sayings that open the Sermon on the Mount ([[Matt.5.3-Matt.5.11|Matthew 5:3–11]]).
God’s right and power to rule and to choose freely, answering to no one.
Pennies.

The king in Jesus’ story forgave his servant a vast debt (“I forgave thee all that debt”), but the servant then refused to forgive a fellow servant a small one ([[Matt.18.32-Matt.18.33|Matthew 18:32–33]]).

modern: The book of Proverbs is also a book of promises. Promises ought to be proverbs among the people of God. This is a very remarkable one. We’re used to thinking of our good things as waiting for us in the future, but here we’re told that we’ll have them in possession.

All the malice and cunning of our enemies can’t bring about our destruction: they’ll fall into the pit they have dug. Our inheritance is so firmly settled on us that we won’t be kept out of it, or turned so far off the path that we miss it.

But what do we have now? We have a quiet conscience through the precious blood of Jesus. We have the love of God set on us beyond all change. We have power with God in prayer whenever we need it. We have the providence of God to watch over us, the angels of God to serve us, and above all the Spirit of God to live in us. In fact, all things are ours. “Whether things present or things to come: all are yours.” Jesus is ours. Yes, the divine Trinity in Unity is ours. Hallelujah. Let’s not mope and whine, and scrimp and slave, since we have good things in possession. Let’s live on our God and rejoice in him all day long. Help us, O Holy Spirit!

notes.note: Property that will come to someone later, once another person’s claim ends: promised, but not yet in hand.
In hand now.

notes.term: The pit which they have digged
notes.note: The verse begins, “Whoso causeth the righteous to go astray in an evil way, he shall fall himself into his own pit” ([[Prov.28.10|Proverbs 28:10]]). Digged is an old form of dug.
An old legal term for an estate fixed to pass down a family line, which could never be sold off or taken away.
Like Jacob, who “had power with God” when he wrestled for a blessing ([[Gen.32.28|Genesis 32:28]]).
God’s care and control over everything that happens, providing for his people.
Serve. Angels are “ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation” ([[Heb.1.14|Hebrews 1:14]]).
“All things are yours; whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours” ([[1Cor.3.21-1Cor.3.22|1 Corinthians 3:21–22]]).
Pine: mope and waste away. Stint: hold back; skimp.
An older name for the Holy Spirit. “Ghost” once meant spirit.

modern: Yes, those wasted years we sigh over will be given back to us. God can give us such plentiful grace that we’ll pack into the rest of our days enough service to make up in some measure for those years before we were born again, which we mourn over in humble repentance.

We now see the locusts of backsliding, worldliness and lukewarmness as a terrible plague. Oh, if only they had never come near us! In mercy the Lord has now taken them away, and we’re full of zeal to serve him. Blessed be his name, we can raise such harvests of spiritual graces that our former barrenness will disappear. Through rich grace we can put our bitter experience to good use, and use it to warn others. Because of our past failures we can become all the more rooted in humility, childlike dependence and repentant spirituality. If we’re more watchful, zealous and tender for it, we’ll gain by our sad losses. The wasted years, by a miracle of love, can be restored. Does that seem too great a gift? Let’s believe for it and live for it, and we may yet see it happen, just as Peter became a far more useful man after his overconfidence was cured by discovering how weak he was. Lord, help us by your grace.

notes.term: The years that the locust hath eaten
notes.note: Joel’s prophecy came after a plague of locusts had stripped the land ([[Joel.2.25|Joel 2:25]]).
Repayment; making up for something.
The state of not yet being born again.
Sorrow for sin that turns away from it.
Drifting back from God into sin.
Being neither hot nor cold toward God ([[Rev.3.16|Revelation 3:16]]).
Put to good use.
Sad; regrettable.
A gift or favor.
Taking things for granted; overconfidence. Peter boasted that he would never deny Jesus, then denied him three times ([[Matt.26.33-Matt.26.35|Matthew 26:33–35]]).

modern: Poor Jeremiah! Yet why do we say that? The weeping prophet was one of God’s choicest servants, and honored by him above many. He was hated for speaking the truth. The word that was so sweet to him was bitter to those who heard it, yet he was accepted by his Lord. He was commanded to stay faithful, and then the Lord would go on speaking through him. He was to deal boldly and truthfully with people, and do the Lord’s work of sifting the professing believers of his day; and then the Lord gave him this word: “Thou shalt be as my mouth.”

What an honor! Shouldn’t every preacher, and indeed every believer, long for it? For God to speak through us: what a marvel! We’ll speak sure, pure truth, and we’ll speak it with power. Our word won’t come back empty; it will be a blessing to those who receive it, and those who refuse it will do so at their peril. Our lips will feed many. We’ll wake the sleeping and call the dead to life.
Oh, dear reader, pray that it may be so with all the servants our Lord sends out.

notes.term: Take forth the precious from the vile
notes.note: Separate what is valuable from what is worthless, the way metal is refined ([[Jer.15.19|Jeremiah 15:19]]).
Jeremiah’s name, from his tears over his people ([[Jer.9.1|Jeremiah 9:1]]).

notes.term: The word which was so sweet to him
notes.note: “Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart” ([[Jer.15.16|Jeremiah 15:16]]).
Tossing grain in the wind so the light husks blow away; sorting the true from the false.
People who publicly claim to be Christians; here, those in Jeremiah’s day who claimed to follow the Lord.
Long for. Usually a sin, but Paul says, “covet earnestly the best gifts” ([[1Cor.12.31|1 Corinthians 12:31]]).
“My word… shall not return unto me void” ([[Isa.55.11|Isaiah 55:11]]).
“The lips of the righteous feed many” ([[Prov.10.21|Proverbs 10:21]]).

modern: This was for Cyrus, but it’s always the inheritance of all the Lord’s own spiritual servants. Only let’s go forward by faith, and our way will be cleared for us. The twists and turns of human craftiness and Satan’s cunning will be straightened for us; we won’t need to follow their winding paths. The gates of brass will be broken, and the iron bars that fastened them will be cut through. We won’t need the battering ram or the crowbar: the Lord himself will do the impossible for us, and the unexpected will become fact.

Let’s not sit down in cowardly fear. Let’s press on in the path of duty; for the Lord has said it: “I will go before thee.” Ours not to reason why; ours only to dare and dash forward. It’s the Lord’s work, and he’ll enable us to do it; every obstacle must give way before him. Hasn’t he said, “I will break in pieces the gates of brass”? What can hinder his purpose or block his decrees? Those who serve God have infinite resources. The way is clear to faith, though barred to human strength. When Jehovah says “I will,” as he does twice in this promise, we dare not doubt.

notes.note: The Persian king who conquered Babylon and let the Jews go home. God named him through Isaiah long before he was born ([[Isa.45.1|Isaiah 45:1]]).
Bronze, or copper.
Into pieces; apart.
Cunning.
An echo of Tennyson’s poem “The Charge of the Light Brigade” (1854): “Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die.”
Obstacles.
Block; thwart.
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.

modern: Why, then, are we afraid of the clouds that now darken our sky? It’s true that for a while they hide the sun, but the sun hasn’t gone out; it will shine again before long. Meanwhile those black clouds are full of rain; and the blacker they are, the more likely they are to give plentiful showers. How can we have rain without clouds?

Our troubles have always brought us blessings, and they always will. They’re the dark chariots of bright grace. These clouds will empty themselves before long, and every tender plant will be the gladder for the shower. Our God may drench us with grief, but he won’t drown us with anger; no, he’ll refresh us with mercy. Our Lord’s love letters often come to us in black-edged envelopes. His wagons rumble, but they’re loaded with blessings. His rod blossoms with sweet flowers and nourishing fruit. Let’s not worry about the clouds, but sing, because May flowers are brought to us through April clouds and showers.

O Lord, the clouds are the dust of your feet! How near you are on the cloudy and dark day! Love sees you and is glad. Faith sees the clouds emptying themselves and making the little hills rejoice on every side.

notes.note: Put out, as a fire is.
Any green plant.
Anger.
In Spurgeon’s day, a letter bringing news of a death came in an envelope with a black border.
God’s discipline, the way a father corrects a child. Spurgeon’s rod that blossoms recalls Aaron’s rod, which budded, blossomed and bore almonds ([[Num.17.8|Numbers 17:8]]).

notes.term: The clouds are the dust of thy feet
notes.note: “The LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet” ([[Nah.1.3|Nahum 1:3]]).
“The little hills rejoice on every side” ([[Ps.65.12|Psalm 65:12]]).

modern: Wretched walking, in the midst of trouble? No, blessed walking, since there’s a special promise for it. Give me a promise, and what is the trouble? What does my Lord teach me to say here? Why, this: “Thou wilt revive me.” I’ll have more life, more energy, more faith. Isn’t it often the case that trouble revives us, like a breath of cold air when someone is about to faint?

How angry my enemies are, and especially the archenemy! Shall I stretch out my hand and fight my foes? No, my hand is better used doing service for my Lord. Besides, there’s no need, for my God will use his far-reaching arm, and he’ll deal with them far better than I could if I tried. “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” With his own right hand of power and wisdom he will save me; and what more can I want?

Come, my heart, talk this promise over with yourself until you can use it as the song of your confidence and the comfort of your loneliness. Pray to be revived yourself, and leave the rest with the Lord, who does all things for you.

notes.note: Anger.
Give new life to.
The chief enemy: Satan.
Comfort.

notes.term: Who performeth all things for thee
notes.note: “I will cry unto God most high; unto God that performeth all things for me” ([[Ps.57.2|Psalm 57:2]]).

modern: The needy man cries out; what else can he do? God hears his cry; what else does he need to do? Let the needy reader start crying out at once, for that will be wisdom. Don’t cry in the ears of friends, for even if they can help you, it’s only because the Lord enables them. The shortest way is to go straight to God and let your cry come up before him. Going straight ahead makes the best runner: run to the Lord, not to secondary causes.

“Alas!” you cry, “I have no friend or helper.” So much the better; you can rely on God on both counts, as one without supplies and without helpers. Make your double need your double plea. You may wait on God even for earthly mercies, for he cares for his children in these passing concerns. As for spiritual needs, which are the heaviest of all, the Lord will hear your cry, and will rescue you and supply you.

Oh, poor friend, try your rich God. Oh, helpless one, lean on his help. He has never failed me, and I’m sure he’ll never fail you. Come as a beggar, and God won’t refuse you help. Come with no plea but his grace. Jesus is King; will he let you die of want? What! Did you forget this?

notes.note: Deliver means rescue. “He shall deliver the needy when he crieth; the poor also, and him that hath no helper” ([[Ps.72.12|Psalm 72:12]]).
An old saying: the runner who heads straight for the finish wins.
The people and things God works through, as opposed to God himself, the first cause of all.
Roles; ways of being.
Belonging to this life; earthly.
An argument offered in a request.
Need; poverty.

modern: Why count heads? One man with God is a majority, even with a thousand on the other side. Sometimes our helpers may be too many for God to work with, as was the case with Gideon, who could do nothing until he had increased his forces by thinning out their numbers. But the Lord’s armies are never too few. When God wanted to found a nation, he called Abram alone and blessed him. When he wanted to defeat proud Pharaoh, he used no armies, but only Moses and Aaron. The “one man ministry,” as certain wise men call it, has been used by the Lord far more than trained regiments with their officers. Did all the Israelites together kill as many as Samson did alone? Saul and his armies killed their thousands, but David his ten thousands.

The Lord can give the enemy long odds and still beat him. If we have faith, we have God with us; and what are multitudes of men? One shepherd’s dog can drive a great flock of sheep before him. If the Lord sent you, my friend, his strength will accomplish his divine purpose. So rely on the promise, and be very courageous.

notes.term: One man of you shall chase a thousand
notes.note: Joshua’s farewell reminder to Israel ([[Josh.23.10|Joshua 23:10]]).
God cut Gideon’s army from thirty-two thousand men to three hundred, so that Israel couldn’t boast that its own strength had saved it ([[Judg.7.2-Judg.7.7|Judges 7:2–7]]).
Armies.
“I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him” ([[Isa.51.2|Isaiah 51:2]]).
Defeat.
A sneering name, used by some in Spurgeon’s day, for a church led by one preacher.
Citizen militia regiments.
With the jawbone of a donkey, Samson alone killed a thousand Philistines ([[Judg.15.15|Judges 15:15]]).
“Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” ([[1Sam.18.7|1 Samuel 18:7]]).
A big advantage in numbers.

modern: This refers first of all to the rain. The Lord will give it in its season. Rain is the picture of all the heavenly refreshment the Lord is ready to give his people. Oh, for a pouring shower to refresh the Lord’s inheritance!

We seem to think God’s treasury can only be opened by a great prophet like Elijah, but it isn’t so, for this promise is to all the faithful in Israel, and in fact to each one of them. Oh, believing friend, “the Lord shall open unto thee his good treasure.” You too may see heaven opened, and thrust in your hand and take out your share; yes, and a share for all your brothers and sisters around you. Ask whatever you want, and you won’t be refused, if you remain in Christ and his words remain in you.

You haven’t yet known all your Lord’s treasures, but he’ll open them up to your understanding. You certainly haven’t yet enjoyed the fullness of his covenant riches, but he’ll direct your heart into his love and reveal Jesus in you. Only the Lord himself can do this for you; but here is his promise, and if you’ll listen carefully to his voice and obey his will, his riches in glory by Christ Jesus will be yours.

notes.note: “The LORD shall open unto thee his good treasure, the heaven to give the rain unto thy land in his season” ([[Deut.28.12|Deuteronomy 28:12]]).
A picture or symbol.
Plentiful.
Inheritance; here, God’s people, his own possession.
Elijah prayed, and it didn’t rain for three and a half years; he prayed again, and the rain came ([[Jas.5.17-Jas.5.18|James 5:17–18]]).
A share of an inheritance. When God is “our portion”, he himself is what we inherit, and he is enough.
Brothers and sisters in Christ.
“If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you” ([[John.15.7|John 15:7]]).

notes.term: Direct thine heart into his love
notes.note: “The Lord direct your hearts into the love of God” ([[2Thess.3.5|2 Thessalonians 3:5]]).
Listen.
“My God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus” ([[Phil.4.19|Philippians 4:19]]).

modern: What a promise this is! To serve God is a high delight in itself. But what an added privilege to have the Lord’s blessing resting on us in everything! Our most ordinary things become blessed when we ourselves are dedicated to the Lord. Our Lord Jesus took bread and blessed it; look, we too eat blessed bread. Jesus blessed water and made it wine: the water we drink is far better to us than any of the wine people make merry with; every drop has a blessing in it. The divine blessing is on the man of God in everything, and it will stay with him at all times.

What if we have only bread and water? Still, it’s blessed bread and water. Bread and water we will have. That’s implied, for it must be there for God to bless it. “Thy bread shall be given thee, and thy waters shall be sure.” With God at our table, we don’t just ask a blessing; we have one. He blesses us not only at the altar but at the table. He serves well those who serve him well. This blessing at the table isn’t something he owes us, but a gift of grace. In fact, there’s a triple grace here: he gives us grace to serve him, by his grace he feeds us with bread, and then in his grace he blesses it.

notes.note: “Ye shall serve the LORD your God, and he shall bless thy bread, and thy water” ([[Exod.23.25|Exodus 23:25]]).
Given wholly to God.
As at the Last Supper ([[Matt.26.26|Matthew 26:26]]).
At the wedding in Cana ([[John.2.7-John.2.9|John 2:7–9]]).
A blessing.
“Bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure” ([[Isa.33.16|Isaiah 33:16]]).

notes.term: Not of debt, but of grace
notes.note: Not owed to us, but freely given ([[Rom.4.4|Romans 4:4]]).
A misprint for “a trebled grace”: a threefold grace, as the next words show.

modern: If we want to glorify our Lord by bearing fruit, we must have certain things inside us; for nothing can come out of us that isn’t first inside us. We must begin with faith, which is the foundation of all the virtues, and then diligently add to it virtue, knowledge, self-control and patience. Along with these we must have godliness and brotherly love. All of these together will most certainly make us produce clusters of usefulness as the fruit of our life, and we won’t be mere idle knowers, but real doers of the Word. These holy things must not only be in us, but abound, or we’ll be barren. Fruit is the overflow of life, and we must be full before we can overflow.

We have noticed men of considerable talents and opportunities who have never succeeded in doing real good in the conversion of souls; and after close observation, we’ve concluded that they lacked certain graces that are absolutely essential to bearing fruit. For real usefulness, graces are better than gifts. As the man is, so is his work. If we want to do better, we must be better. Let this text be a gentle hint to fruitless professing Christians, and to me as well.

notes.note: The heading has lost a syllable: the King James Version reads “neither be barren nor unfruitful” ([[2Pet.1.8|2 Peter 1:8]]).

“Add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; and to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; and to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity” ([[2Pet.1.5-2Pet.1.7|2 Peter 1:5–7]]).
Self-control.
“Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only” ([[Jas.1.22|James 1:22]]).
Be present in plenty; overflow.
Talents; abilities.
Graces are the Spirit’s fruit in a person’s character, such as love, humility and faith; gifts are abilities, such as preaching or learning.
People who publicly claim to be Christians.

modern: This is the sure way of winning with the Lord in prayer. We may humbly remind him of what he has said. Our faithful God will never go back on his word, or leave it unfulfilled; yet he loves to be asked by his people and reminded of his promise. This refreshes their memories, revives their faith and renews their hope. God’s Word is given not for his sake but for ours. His purposes are settled, and he needs nothing to bind him to his plan of doing his people good; but he gives the promise to strengthen and comfort us. So he wants us to plead it, and say to him, “Thou saidst.”

“I will surely do thee good” is the very essence of all the Lord’s gracious sayings. Put special stress on the word “surely.” He will do us good: real good, lasting good, only good, every good. He will make us good, and that is doing us good in the very highest degree. He will treat us as he treats his saints while we’re here, and that is good. He will soon take us to be with Jesus and all his chosen, and that is supremely good. With this promise in our hearts we needn’t fear angry Esau, or anyone else. If the Lord will do us good, who can do us harm?

notes.term: Thou saidst, I will surely do thee good
notes.note: Jacob’s prayer on the night before he met his brother Esau, who was coming with four hundred men ([[Gen.32.9-Gen.32.12|Genesis 32:9–12]]).
Winning; succeeding. That night Jacob wrestled with God and “prevailed” ([[Gen.32.28|Genesis 32:28]]).
Asked. “I will yet for this be enquired of by the house of Israel, to do it for them” ([[Ezek.36.37|Ezekiel 36:37]]).
Present as an argument in prayer.
“Who is he that will harm you, if ye be followers of that which is good?” ([[1Pet.3.13|1 Peter 3:13]]).

modern: Only by following Jesus can we get our heart’s desire and be really useful to our fellow men. Oh, how we long to be successful fishers for Jesus! We’d give our lives to win souls. But we’re tempted to try methods Jesus would never have tried. Shall we give in to this suggestion of the enemy? If so, we may splash the water, but we’ll never catch the fish. We must follow Jesus if we want to succeed. Sensational methods, entertainments and so on: is that following Jesus? Can we imagine the Lord Jesus drawing a congregation by the means that are commonly used now? What comes of such schemes? Nothing that Jesus will count on the last great day.

We must stick to our preaching, as our Master did, for this is how souls are saved. We must preach our Lord’s teaching and proclaim a full and free gospel, for this is the net that catches souls. We must preach with his gentleness, boldness and love, for this is the secret of success with human hearts. We must work under the divine anointing, depending on the Holy Spirit. So, following Jesus, and not running ahead of him or off to the side of him, we’ll be fishers of men.

notes.note: Jesus’ call to the fishermen Simon and Andrew ([[Mark.1.16-Mark.1.17|Mark 1:16–17]]).
Attention-grabbing shows and stunts to draw a crowd.
Quick fixes; schemes that work for now.
The day of judgment.
The Holy Spirit’s power resting on a preacher ([[1John.2.27|1 John 2:27]]).

modern: Ah, Lord, you were at your lowest when you were made to stand before your persecutors like a criminal! Yet the eyes of your faith could see beyond your present humiliation into your future glory. What words these are: “Nevertheless—hereafter”! I want to imitate your holy foresight, and in the middle of poverty or sickness or slander, I too would say, “Nevertheless—hereafter.” Instead of weakness, you have all power; instead of shame, all glory; instead of mockery, all worship. Your cross hasn’t dimmed the splendor of your crown, and the spit hasn’t spoiled the beauty of your face. Rather, you’re all the more exalted and honored because of your sufferings.

So, Lord, I too would take courage from the “hereafter.” I would forget the present trouble in the future triumph. Help me by directing me into your Father’s love and into your own patience, so that when I’m mocked for your name, I may not be shaken, but may think more and more of the hereafter, and so all the less of today. I’ll be with you soon and see your glory. So I’m not ashamed, but say in my inmost soul, “Nevertheless—hereafter.”

notes.note: From now on; in the time to come. Jesus’ answer to the high priest at his trial ([[Matt.26.63-Matt.26.64|Matthew 26:63–64]]).
Mockery.
“Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him” ([[Matt.26.67|Matthew 26:67]]).
Trouble, suffering.

notes.term: Directing me into thy Father’s love
notes.note: “The Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patient waiting for Christ” ([[2Thess.3.5|2 Thessalonians 3:5]]).
Shaken.
“Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory” ([[John.17.24|John 17:24]]).
“For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed” ([[2Tim.1.12|2 Timothy 1:12]]).

modern: My Lord’s words are true about the tribulation. I have my share of it, beyond all doubt. The flail isn’t hung up out of the way, and I can’t hope it will be laid aside as long as I lie on the threshing floor. How can I expect to be at home in the enemy’s country, joyful in exile, or comfortable in a wilderness? This is not my rest. This is the place of the furnace, the forge and the hammer. My experience matches my Lord’s words.

I notice how he tells me to “be of good cheer.” Sadly, I’m far too inclined to be downcast. My spirit soon sinks when I’m sorely tried. But I mustn’t give in to this feeling. When my Lord tells me to cheer up, I mustn’t dare to be cast down.

What argument does he use to encourage me? Why, his own victory. He says, “I have overcome the world.” His battle was much harder than mine. I haven’t yet resisted to the point of shedding blood. Why do I despair of overcoming? Look, my soul, the enemy has been overcome once already. I’m fighting a beaten foe. O world, Jesus has already conquered you; and in me, by his grace, he’ll overcome you again. So I’m of good cheer, and I sing to my conquering Lord.

notes.note: Trouble, suffering.
A tool for threshing grain: a short stick swinging from a long handle, beaten on the grain to knock it out of the husks.
The hard floor where grain was beaten out.
“Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest” ([[Mic.2.10|Micah 2:10]]).
Matches.
Cheer up; take heart.
“Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin” ([[Heb.12.4|Hebrews 12:4]]).
Defeated.
